classification.difficultyReason: Explains a counting interpretation by matching initial values and the recursive addition rule.

content.prompt: An alternative interpretation of Pascal’s triangle is that its entries count the number of paths from the top of the triangle to the position of the entry (with the understanding that we only move downwards to the left or downwards to the right at each step along the paths). Explain why this is so.

answer.short:
Path counts start at 1 and obey the same addition rule as Pascal’s triangle.

Each interior position receives paths from the two positions immediately above it; each edge position has just one path.
answer.worked:
There is one path from the top to itself, agreeing with $\binom{0}{0}=1$. Each edge position also has exactly one path, agreeing with the outer entries of Pascal’s triangle.

Every path to an interior position arrives from either the position immediately above left or the position immediately above right. These two groups of paths are disjoint, so their counts add.

Thus the path counts start with the same top entry and satisfy the same rule as Pascal’s Identity, $\binom{n}{k}=\binom{n-1}{k-1}+\binom{n-1}{k}$. Row by row, the path counts therefore equal the entries of Pascal’s triangle.
